newsitem.title: FRANCE: Scientology rejoices, opponents slam French ruling.
newsitem.headline: Scientology rejoices, opponents slam French ruling.

text.p: The Church of Scientology rejoiced on Tuesday after a French court recognised it as a religion but detractors denounced the church as a dangerous sect and accused the judges of exceeding their powers.

The appeals court in the central France city of Lyon acquitted nine people and reduced sentences for six others on Monday, including the former head of the Church of Scientology in Lyon who was convicted of manslaughter and fraud.

It caused most controversy by ruling that "the Church of Scientology can rightfully claim to be a religion and develop in total freedom, within the framework of existing laws, its missionary activities and even proselytise".
A French parliamentary report in 1996 described Scientology as a "sect", undermining claims to respectability and damaging its fundraising.

The head of the Church of Scientology, Reverend Heber Jentzsch, said in Los Angeles the ruling was "a dream come true for my church and minority religions...Despite political pressure and hysteria promoting a new inquisition, the court has returned to the French tradition of liberty and equality".

Civil plaintiffs and opponents of the church decried the court ruling. They stressed that it upheld manslaughter and fraud convictions against the ex-head of the Lyon branch, Jean-Jacques Mazier, after the 1988 death of a follower.

"This trial has made more and more people aware that Scientology is a dangerous sect, that it is a sect that has infiltrated all the institutions of our society," said Jeannine Tavernier, president of the UNADFI, an anti-sect organisation.
"Is it the role of a court to decide between sect or religion? We are astonished," she said.

Germany, for instance, does not recognise Scientology as a religion, seeing it as a business to exploit the gullible. Scientologists have compared Bonn's treatment of the church to Hitler's treatment of the Jews before World War Two.
Washington has expressed concern about German discrimination while rejecting Scientologists' comparisons with the Nazis.

The Lyon court handed Mazier a three-year suspended term and fined him 500,000 francs ($80,000) on charges of manslaughter and fraud over the 1988 suicide of Scientology follower Patrice Vic, a 31-year-old industrial designer.

A lower court in October sentenced Mazier to 18 months in jail, with another 18 months suspended, ruling he put pressure on Vic to raise cash to attend Scientology courses. Unable to raise the money, Vic threw himself out of a high-rise block.
The prosecutor said he would appeal the new verdict.
Jean-Pierre Brard, a French parliamentarian who helped write a report on sects in France, described Scientology as "one of the most dangerous sects that exist".

"A court is expected to protect its citizens' freedoms, but what has happened is the opposite," he said. Scientology was founded in 1954 by the late American science-fiction novelist L. Ron Hubbard and claims more than eight million members worldwide.

One of its teachings is that the problems of the human race are linked to disembodied souls brought to the planet millions of years ago. Members include Hollywood film stars Tom Cruise, his Australian-born wife Nicole Kidman, John Travolta, Kirstie Alley and Lisa Marie Presley, daughter of late rock star Elvis Presley.

While saying the church could be seen as a religion, the appeals court also said the local Scientology leaders had "made their church into a money-gathering enterprise to the detriment of their followers".

It acquitted nine of 14 other defendants tied to the Church sentenced with Mazier. The five other defendants also received lighter sentences ranging from eight months to one year suspended with fines from 10,000 to 20,000 francs.
